entities.name: Jean Crespin
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean Crespin (died April 22, 1572), a French Protestant émigré and lawyer by training, established himself as a pivotal printer and chronicler of religious persecution in Geneva during the mid-16th century. Fleeing persecution in his native France, his press became a central hub for Reformed theology and anti-Catholic polemic, playing a crucial role in documenting the suffering and fortitude of Protestant martyrs. His most enduring work, the *Histoire des martyrs persécutés et mis à mort pour la vérité de l'Évangile*, commonly known as the *Livre des Martyrs*, served not only as a meticulously gathered historical record but also as a powerful propaganda tool, solidifying the identity and resolve of the nascent Protestant movement across Europe amidst the tumultuous Wars of Religion.

Originally practicing law in Arras, Crespin converted to Protestantism, an act that led to his forced exile from France around 1545. He subsequently settled in Geneva, a burgeoning center of the Reformation, where he commenced his printing career in 1548. His Geneva press quickly became one of the most prolific publishers of Reformed literature, producing hundreds of editions, including seminal works by John Calvin, Theodore Beza, and other leading Reformers, alongside Bibles and theological treatises. His magnum opus, first published in 1554 and significantly expanded in subsequent editions (e.g., 1564, 1570), painstakingly detailed the trials, executions, and testimonies of thousands of Protestants, from the Waldensians of the 12th century to those persecuted under Francis I and Henry II.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jean Crespin's *Livre des Martyrs* became a foundational text for Protestant identity, documenting over 1,500 martyrdoms and inspiring generations of Reformed communities. His printing press in Geneva was a key conduit for spreading Reformed theology across Europe during the 16th century.
